nodes.title: Introduction to energy production in the mitochondria
nodes.canonical_question: How do mitochondria produce energy for the cell?
nodes.summary: Cellular respiration converts nutrients into ATP. Most ATP is made in the mitochondrion.

nodes.title: ATP synthase mechanism
nodes.canonical_question: How does ATP synthase use proton flow to make ATP?
nodes.summary: Protons flow through the F0 rotor, spinning the stalk. The F1 head cycles through conformations that bind ADP and phosphate and release ATP.

nodes.title: Inner mitochondrial membrane role
nodes.canonical_question: Why is the inner mitochondrial membrane important for ATP production?
nodes.summary: The inner membrane is impermeable to protons. This forces protons through ATP synthase, coupling the gradient to ATP production.

nodes.title: NADH and FADH2 as electron donors
nodes.canonical_question: How do NADH and FADH2 feed electrons into the transport chain?
nodes.summary: NADH donates electrons at Complex I; FADH2 at Complex II. Each donation ultimately pumps protons across the membrane.

nodes.title: Glycolysis yield and mitochondrial input
nodes.canonical_question: How much ATP does glycolysis produce and how does it feed the mitochondrion?
nodes.summary: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH in the cytoplasm. Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is converted to acetyl-CoA.

nodes.title: Mitochondrial cristae surface area
nodes.canonical_question: Why do mitochondria have inner membrane folds called cristae?
nodes.summary: Cristae dramatically increase inner membrane surface area. More surface means more ATP synthase complexes and higher ATP output.

nodes.title: Oxygen as the final electron acceptor
nodes.canonical_question: Why does the electron transport chain require oxygen?
nodes.summary: Oxygen accepts the final electrons at Complex IV, forming water. Without oxygen the chain stalls and ATP production stops.

nodes.title: Krebs cycle connection to electron transport
nodes.canonical_question: How does the Krebs cycle supply electrons to the transport chain?
nodes.summary: Each acetyl-CoA through the Krebs cycle yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 GTP. These carriers feed the electron transport chain.

nodes.title: Total ATP yield from one glucose molecule
nodes.canonical_question: How many ATP molecules can one glucose molecule produce through aerobic respiration?
nodes.summary: Complete oxidation of one glucose can yield approximately 30-32 ATP under cellular conditions via glycolysis, Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.

nodes.title: Mitochondrial double membrane
nodes.canonical_question: What is the function of each mitochondrial membrane layer?
nodes.summary: The outer membrane is permeable via porins. The inner membrane is tight, creating the intermembrane space where protons accumulate.

nodes.title: Chemiosmosis definition
nodes.canonical_question: What is chemiosmosis and how does it generate ATP?
nodes.summary: Chemiosmosis is the use of an electrochemical gradient across a membrane to drive ATP synthesis. Proton flow through ATP synthase releases energy.

nodes.title: Reactive oxygen species from the transport chain
nodes.canonical_question: How does the electron transport chain generate reactive oxygen species?
nodes.summary: Electrons occasionally leak from Complexes I and III to oxygen, forming superoxide. Cells use antioxidant enzymes to neutralise these radicals.

nodes.title: ATP use in active transport
nodes.canonical_question: How do cells use ATP to power active transport across membranes?
nodes.summary: Membrane pumps like the sodium-potassium ATPase hydrolyse ATP to move ions against their concentration gradient.

nodes.title: Mitochondrial endosymbiotic origin
nodes.canonical_question: What is the endosymbiotic theory of mitochondrial origin?
nodes.summary: An ancestral eukaryotic cell engulfed an aerobic bacterium. Over time this became a permanent endosymbiont, retaining its own DNA and double membrane.

nodes.title: Anaerobic respiration versus aerobic
nodes.canonical_question: Why does anaerobic respiration produce far less ATP than aerobic respiration?
nodes.summary: Without the electron transport chain, cells rely on substrate-level phosphorylation only, yielding just 2 ATP per glucose instead of ~30.

nodes.title: Mitochondria as semi-autonomous organelles
nodes.canonical_question: Why are mitochondria considered semi-autonomous organelles?
nodes.summary: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and ribosomes and divide by binary fission. But most of their proteins are nuclear-encoded and imported.

nodes.title: Proton gradient formation by Complex I
nodes.canonical_question: How does Complex I pump protons across the inner membrane?
nodes.summary: Complex I couples NADH oxidation to proton pumping via a long hydrophobic arm. Four protons are translocated per NADH.

nodes.title: F1 catalytic head conformational cycling
nodes.canonical_question: What are the three conformational states of the F1 head during ATP synthesis?
nodes.summary: The F1 beta subunits cycle through open, loose, and tight states. ADP and Pi bind in the loose state; ATP is released from the tight state.

nodes.title: Complex IV and oxygen reduction
nodes.canonical_question: How does Complex IV transfer electrons to oxygen and what is the product?
nodes.summary: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) passes four electrons to one oxygen molecule, producing two water molecules and pumping four protons.

nodes.title: Cytochrome c structure and role
nodes.canonical_question: What does cytochrome c do in the electron transport chain?
nodes.summary: Cytochrome c is a small mobile electron carrier. It shuttles electrons from Complex III to Complex IV.

nodes.title: Mitochondrial ATP generation overview
nodes.canonical_question: What process do mitochondria use to generate ATP for the cell?
nodes.summary: Cellular respiration converts nutrients into ATP. Most ATP is made in the mitochondrion.

nodes.title: ATP synthase proton-driven synthesis
nodes.canonical_question: How does the flow of protons through ATP synthase produce ATP molecules?
nodes.summary: Protons flow through the F0 rotor, spinning the stalk. The F1 head cycles through conformations that bind ADP and phosphate and release ATP.

nodes.title: Inner membrane and ATP coupling
nodes.canonical_question: What role does the inner membrane of the mitochondrion play in ATP synthesis?
nodes.summary: The inner membrane is impermeable to protons. This forces protons through ATP synthase, coupling the gradient to ATP production.

nodes.title: Electron-carrier input to respiratory chain
nodes.canonical_question: How do the electron carriers NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the respiratory chain?
nodes.summary: NADH donates electrons at Complex I; FADH2 at Complex II. Each donation ultimately pumps protons across the membrane.

nodes.title: Glycolysis ATP and pyruvate entry
nodes.canonical_question: What is the ATP yield of glycolysis and how does pyruvate enter the mitochondrion?
nodes.summary: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH in the cytoplasm. Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is converted to acetyl-CoA.

nodes.title: Cristae function in energy output
nodes.canonical_question: What is the function of cristae in the inner mitochondrial membrane?
nodes.summary: Cristae dramatically increase inner membrane surface area. More surface means more ATP synthase complexes and higher ATP output.

nodes.title: Oxygen requirement for electron transport
nodes.canonical_question: What is the role of oxygen in the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
nodes.summary: Oxygen accepts the final electrons at Complex IV, forming water. Without oxygen the chain stalls and ATP production stops.

nodes.title: Krebs cycle electron carrier production
nodes.canonical_question: What electron carriers does the Krebs cycle produce for the electron transport chain?
nodes.summary: Each acetyl-CoA through the Krebs cycle yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 GTP. These carriers feed the electron transport chain.

nodes.title: ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration
nodes.canonical_question: What is the total ATP yield when one glucose is fully oxidised in aerobic respiration?
nodes.summary: Complete oxidation of one glucose can yield approximately 30-32 ATP under cellular conditions via glycolysis, Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.

nodes.title: Outer versus inner mitochondrial membrane
nodes.canonical_question: How do the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes differ in structure and function?
nodes.summary: The outer membrane is permeable via porins. The inner membrane is tight, creating the intermembrane space where protons accumulate.

nodes.title: Electrochemical gradient ATP coupling
nodes.canonical_question: In cellular energy production, how is a concentration difference of hydrogen ions across a membrane used to synthesise adenosine triphosphate?
nodes.summary: Chemiosmosis is the use of an electrochemical gradient across a membrane to drive ATP synthesis. Proton flow through ATP synthase releases energy.

nodes.title: Radical oxygen escape during respiration
nodes.canonical_question: During oxidative phosphorylation, under what circumstances do partially reduced oxygen molecules escape as harmful radicals?
nodes.summary: Electrons occasionally leak from Complexes I and III to oxygen, forming superoxide. Cells use antioxidant enzymes to neutralise these radicals.

nodes.title: ATP hydrolysis driving ion pumps
nodes.canonical_question: In membrane biology, how do ion pumps couple adenosine triphosphate hydrolysis to moving substances against their concentration gradients?
nodes.summary: Membrane pumps like the sodium-potassium ATPase hydrolyse ATP to move ions against their concentration gradient.

nodes.title: Bacterial ancestor of the mitochondrion
nodes.canonical_question: How does the hypothesis that an ancient cell absorbed a free-living aerobic bacterium explain the two-membrane structure of present-day mitochondria?
nodes.summary: An ancestral eukaryotic cell engulfed an aerobic bacterium. Over time this became a permanent endosymbiont, retaining its own DNA and double membrane.

nodes.title: Oxygen absence and ATP shortfall
nodes.canonical_question: When cells lack access to oxygen, why is the ATP output of glucose breakdown reduced from roughly 30 to just 2 molecules per glucose?
nodes.summary: Without the electron transport chain, cells rely on substrate-level phosphorylation only, yielding just 2 ATP per glucose instead of ~30.

nodes.title: Mitochondria own DNA yet need nucleus
nodes.canonical_question: Given that mitochondria carry circular DNA and divide independently but depend on nuclear genes for most of their proteins, what does this hybrid dependence tell us?
nodes.summary: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and ribosomes and divide by binary fission. But most of their proteins are nuclear-encoded and imported.

nodes.title: NADH dehydrogenase proton translocation
nodes.canonical_question: Describe the structural mechanism by which NADH dehydrogenase couples electron transfer from NADH to the translocation of hydrogen ions across the inner membrane.
nodes.summary: Complex I couples NADH oxidation to proton pumping via a long hydrophobic arm. Four protons are translocated per NADH.

nodes.title: Beta subunit shape changes in F1 motor
nodes.canonical_question: In the rotary mechanism of ATP production, what sequential shape changes of the beta catalytic subunits drive binding of ADP and phosphate and release of ATP?
nodes.summary: The F1 beta subunits cycle through open, loose, and tight states. ADP and Pi bind in the loose state; ATP is released from the tight state.

nodes.title: Cytochrome c oxidase reaction products
nodes.canonical_question: At the terminus of the respiratory chain, how does cytochrome c oxidase reduce molecular oxygen, how many protons does it translocate, and what metabolite is formed?
nodes.summary: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) passes four electrons to one oxygen molecule, producing two water molecules and pumping four protons.

nodes.title: Mobile haem protein in electron relay
nodes.canonical_question: In oxidative phosphorylation, how does the small haem-containing protein that shuttles between two protein complexes participate in electron transfer?
nodes.summary: Cytochrome c is a small mobile electron carrier. It shuttles electrons from Complex III to Complex IV.

nodes.title: ATP synthase assembly regulation
nodes.canonical_question: How is ATP synthase assembly regulated during mitochondrial biogenesis?
nodes.summary: Mitochondrial biogenesis signals coordinate assembly of F0 and F1 subunits. ATPAF chaperones hold F1 subunits until F0 is ready.

nodes.title: Cristae remodelling during apoptosis
nodes.canonical_question: How do mitochondrial cristae remodel during apoptosis and what proteins control this?
nodes.summary: OPA1 oligomers seal crista junctions; during apoptosis BAX/BAK cause junction opening and cytochrome c release.

nodes.title: Hypoxia and ETC gene expression
nodes.canonical_question: How does low oxygen availability affect transcription of electron transport chain subunit genes?
nodes.summary: HIF-1 accumulates under hypoxia and activates genes for glycolysis while suppressing some ETC subunits to reduce ROS production.

nodes.title: Phosphofructokinase allosteric control
nodes.canonical_question: How does phosphofructokinase regulate glycolysis and how does accumulated ATP inhibit the enzyme?
nodes.summary: PFK-1 is allosterically inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP. This makes glycolytic flux respond to the cell energy charge.

nodes.title: Krebs cycle anaplerosis
nodes.canonical_question: How does the Krebs cycle supply biosynthetic precursors for amino acid and lipid synthesis?
nodes.summary: Alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate are drained for amino acid synthesis. Anaplerotic reactions replenish them so the cycle continues.

nodes.title: Mitochondrial DNA replication
nodes.canonical_question: How is mitochondrial DNA replicated and which polymerase carries out this process?
nodes.summary: Mitochondrial DNA uses a strand-displacement mechanism. DNA polymerase gamma (POLG) replicates the heavy strand; the light strand template remains single-stranded.

nodes.title: 2,4-DNP and uncoupling mechanism
nodes.canonical_question: How does 2,4-dinitrophenol collapse the proton gradient and why does it increase oxygen consumption?
nodes.summary: DNP is a proton carrier that shuttles H+ across the inner membrane without ATP synthase, dissipating the gradient as heat.

nodes.title: Malate-aspartate shuttle
nodes.canonical_question: How does the malate-aspartate shuttle transfer cytoplasmic NADH electrons into the mitochondrial matrix?
nodes.summary: Malate carries reducing equivalents across the inner membrane; aspartate carries the spent carbon skeleton back. Net effect is NADH oxidation in the matrix.

nodes.title: Adenine nucleotide translocase
nodes.canonical_question: How does the mitochondrial ADP/ATP translocase exchange matrix ATP for cytosolic ADP?
nodes.summary: ANT (SLC25A4) catalyses electrogenic exchange of one ATP4- for one ADP3- per cycle, driven by the membrane potential.

nodes.title: P/O ratio determination method
nodes.canonical_question: How do researchers measure the P/O ratio of isolated mitochondria experimentally?
nodes.summary: Oxygen electrodes measure O2 consumption; luminometry or HPLC measure ATP produced. The ratio of ATP synthesised to O consumed gives the P/O ratio.
